answer:
The rate of a reaction is written by dividing the rate of change of concentration of each species by its stoichiometric coefficient, with a minus sign on a reactant, whose concentration falls with time, and a plus sign on a product, whose concentration rises.

Reading the given expression term by term:

\(-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt}\) carries a minus sign and the coefficient \(3\), so A is a reactant with coefficient \(3\).

\(+\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}\) carries a plus sign and the coefficient \(2\), so B is a product with coefficient \(2\).

\(+\dfrac{d[\mathrm{C}]}{dt}\) carries a plus sign and the coefficient \(1\), so C is a product with coefficient \(1\).

\(\therefore\) the reaction is \(\mathrm{3A \longrightarrow 2B + C}\)

None of the four printed alternatives is \(\mathrm{3A \longrightarrow 2B + C}\). Each of them would require a different set of signs in the given expression: \(\mathrm{3A + 2B \longrightarrow C}\) needs a minus sign on the B term as well as on the A term; \(\mathrm{2B \longrightarrow 3A + C}\) needs the minus sign on the B term and a plus sign on the A term; and \(\mathrm{2B + C \longrightarrow 3A}\) needs minus signs on the B and the C terms together with a plus sign on the A term. As printed, the question has no correct answer among its alternatives.

answer:
For a zero order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow P}\) the rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant, so

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)

Rearranging and integrating between \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_t\) at time \(t\) gives the integrated rate law

\(k\,t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t\)

The half life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time in which the concentration of the reactant falls to half its initial value, so at \(t = t_{1/2}\) we have \([\mathrm{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\). Substituting this condition,

\(k\,t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\)

\(\therefore t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)  and  \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2\,t_{1/2}}\)

The half life of a zero order reaction is thus directly proportional to the initial concentration of the reactant, unlike that of a first order reaction, which is independent of it.

**Instantaneous rate of reaction.** The instantaneous rate of a reaction is the rate of the reaction at a particular instant of time. It is obtained by replacing the average rate \(\dfrac{\Delta c}{\Delta t}\), measured over an interval, by the derivative \(\dfrac{dc}{dt}\) at that instant, so that for \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow B}\)

instantaneous rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}\)

In practice the concentration of a reactant or a product is measured at a series of times and plotted against time; a tangent is drawn to the curve at the instant of interest, and the slope of that tangent is the instantaneous rate.

**Pseudo first order reaction.** A pseudo first order reaction is a reaction which is expected from its rate law to be of a higher order, but which is found experimentally to follow first order kinetics.

**Example.** The hydrolysis of methyl acetate:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3(aq) + H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow CH_3COOH(aq) + CH_3OH(aq)}\)

Its rate law is

rate \(= k'[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]\)

so the reaction is expected to be of second order. Water is the solvent and is present in such large excess that the quantity consumed during the reaction is negligible compared with the quantity present, so \([\mathrm{H_2O}]\) remains effectively constant. Writing \([\mathrm{H_2O}] = k''\), a constant,

rate \(= k'\,k''\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}] = k\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}]\)  where \(k = k'\,k''\)

The rate now depends on one concentration term only and the reaction follows first order kinetics, so it is a pseudo first order reaction.
twin: What are pseudo-first order reactions? Give one example and explain why it is pseudo-first order.

For a first order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow products}\) the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

Separating the variables,

\(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\,dt\)

Integrating between \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_t\) at time \(t\),

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\(\ln[\mathrm{A}]_t - \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 = -k\,t\), that is \(\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = -k\,t\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

and converting the natural logarithm to base \(10\),

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

which is the integrated rate law for a first order reaction.

Three of the four printed expressions are this one equation written in different ways. Since \(\ln z = 2.303\log_{10} z\) and \(-\ln z = \ln\dfrac{1}{z}\), the forms \(\dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\), \(\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\) and \(-\dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0}\) are all equal to \(k\). The remaining form, \(\dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0}\), has the ratio inverted and is equal to \(-k\); since a rate constant is a positive quantity, it is the only incorrect expression of the four. The alternatives as printed therefore do not single out one answer.

answer:
For a first order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow products}\) the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

Separating the variables and integrating between \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_t\) at time \(t\),

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\(\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = -k\,t\)

so that the integrated rate law is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

**The half life period.** The half life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time required for the concentration of the reactant to fall to one half of its initial value. Hence at \(t = t_{1/2}\),

\([\mathrm{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\)

Substituting this condition into the integrated rate law,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_0/2} = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10} 2\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{t_{1/2}}\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  and  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

The initial concentration \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) has cancelled out of the result, which is why the half life period of a first order reaction is independent of the initial concentration of the reactant.

For a first order reaction the integrated rate law is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

Taking the initial amount of the compound as \(100\), the amount remaining unreacted after \(45\) minutes is \(40\).

\([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\), \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 40\), \(t = 45\ \mathrm{min}\)

Substitution gives

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{45}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{40} = \dfrac{2.303}{45}\log_{10} 2.5\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{45} \times 0.3979\)

\(\therefore k = 0.0204\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} = 2.04 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

Dividing by \(60\) expresses the same rate constant in reciprocal seconds:

\(k = \dfrac{0.0204}{60} = 3.39 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

The value can be checked against the half life it implies, \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0204} = 34\ \mathrm{min}\). The reaction has therefore run for a little longer than one half life, so rather less than half the sample should remain, and the given \(40\%\) is consistent with that.

For \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow products}\) let the order of the reaction be \(n\), so that

rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^n\)   ...... (i)

When the concentration of A is increased by a factor of \(4\) the rate becomes twice as large:

\(2 \times\) rate \(= k\,(4[\mathrm{A}])^n = k\,4^n[\mathrm{A}]^n\)   ...... (ii)

Dividing (ii) by (i), the factor \(k[\mathrm{A}]^n\) cancels:

\(2 = 4^n\)

Writing \(4 = 2^2\) gives \(2^1 = 2^{2n}\), so \(2n = 1\)

\(\therefore n = 0.5\)

The size of the change confirms it. A zero order reaction would not have changed the rate at all, a first order reaction would have made it four times as large and a second order reaction sixteen times as large. Only a fractional order below one produces a mere doubling, and the order of a reaction, being determined by experiment, may be a fraction.

answer:
**Elementary reaction.** An elementary reaction is one which takes place in a single step, exactly as its chemical equation is written. Because the single step is the reaction itself, the exponents in its rate law are the same as the stoichiometric coefficients in its balanced equation, so its order and its molecularity are equal.

An elementary reaction that is first order is therefore unimolecular: one molecule of a single reactant takes part in the one step. The isomerisation of cyclopropane to propene,

\(\mathrm{C_3H_6(g) \longrightarrow CH_3-CH=CH_2(g)}\)

is such a reaction, its rate law being rate \(= k[\mathrm{C_3H_6}]\).

**Complex reaction.** A complex reaction is one which does not take place in a single step but through a sequence of two or more elementary steps. That sequence of steps is the mechanism of the reaction, and a species which is produced in one step and consumed in a later one is a reaction intermediate. The slowest of the steps controls how fast the products can appear and is called the rate determining step.

The order of a complex reaction is decided by experiment and need not bear any relation to the coefficients of the overall balanced equation. The decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide,

\(\mathrm{2\,N_2O_5(g) \longrightarrow 4\,NO_2(g) + O_2(g)}\)

is of this kind: although two molecules appear in the balanced equation, the reaction is found to be first order, its rate law being rate \(= k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]\), because its rate determining step involves a single molecule of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\). A complex reaction is first order whenever its rate determining step involves one molecule of one reactant, so that the experimentally determined rate law contains a single concentration term raised to the first power.

**(A)** \(\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)

For a zero order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow product}\) the rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant, so the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)

Rearranging,

\(d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\,dt\)

Integrating between \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_t\) at time \(t\),

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t} d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\([\mathrm{A}]_t - [\mathrm{A}]_0 = -k\,t\), that is \(k\,t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t\)

At the half life, \(t = t_{1/2}\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\), so

\(k\,t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\)

\(\therefore t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\)

The expression \(\dfrac{0.693}{k}\) is the half life of a first order reaction and carries no concentration term at all, so it cannot serve for a zero order reaction, whose half life must depend on the initial concentration. Of the remaining expressions, both of which contain \([\mathrm{A}]_0\), only the one with \(2k\) in the denominator satisfies the integrated rate law derived above; the form \(\dfrac{2[\mathrm{A}]_0}{k}\) is four times too large.

For a first order reaction the half life period and the rate constant are related by

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)  or  \(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)

\(t_{1/2} = 6.0\ \mathrm{h}\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{0.693}{6.0\ \mathrm{h}} = 0.1155\ \mathrm{h^{-1}} = 1.155 \times 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\)

Expressed in seconds the half life is \(6.0 \times 3600 = 2.16 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s}\), so the same rate constant is

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{2.16 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s}} = 3.21 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

Substituting back, \(\dfrac{0.693}{0.1155\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}} = 6.0\ \mathrm{h}\), which is the half life given in the question.

answer:
**Rate constant: the integrated rate law.** For a first order reaction

\(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow products}\)

the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

Separating the variables,

\(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\,dt\)

Let \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) be the initial concentration of A at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) its concentration at time \(t\). Integrating between these limits,

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\(\ln[\mathrm{A}]_t - \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 = -k\,t\)

\(\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = -k\,t\)

\(k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

Converting the natural logarithm to base \(10\),

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

**Half life.** The half life \(t_{1/2}\) is the time in which the concentration of the reactant falls to one half of its initial value, so at \(t = t_{1/2}\),

\([\mathrm{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\)

Putting this into the expression for \(k\),

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_0/2} = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10} 2 = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.3010}{t_{1/2}}\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  and  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

Because \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) cancels, the half life of a first order reaction does not depend on the initial concentration of the reactant, and the unit of \(k\) is the reciprocal of the unit of time.

**(B)** \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{P_i}{2P_i - P}\)

Consider the first order gas phase reaction

\(\mathrm{A(g) \longrightarrow B(g) + C(g)}\)

Let \(P_i\) be the initial pressure of A, let the pressure of A fall by \(x\) in time \(t\), and let \(P\) be the total pressure of the mixture at that time.

Pressure of A at time \(t\):

\(P_{\mathrm{A}} = P_i - x\)

One mole of A gives one mole of B and one mole of C, so at time \(t\) the pressures of the products are

\(P_{\mathrm{B}} = P_{\mathrm{C}} = x\)

The total pressure at that time is therefore

\(P = (P_i - x) + x + x = P_i + x\)

\(\therefore x = P - P_i\)

Substituting for \(x\) in the pressure of A,

\(P_{\mathrm{A}} = P_i - (P - P_i) = 2P_i - P\)

At constant volume and temperature the concentration of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure, so in the integrated rate law of a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

the concentrations may be replaced by pressures, with \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = P_i\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_t = P_{\mathrm{A}} = 2P_i - P\). Hence

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{P_i}{2P_i - P}\)

where \(P\) is the total pressure of the reaction mixture at time \(t\).

The other expressions fail simple tests. The one with \(P_i - P\) in the denominator makes the ratio negative, because the total pressure rises above \(P_i\) as the reaction proceeds, and the logarithm of a negative quantity does not exist. The one carrying \(2P_i\) where the time belongs cannot be a rate constant at all, since \(k\) must vary inversely with time. The last carries an extra pressure ratio that the derivation above does not produce.

answer:
**Pseudo first order reaction.** A pseudo first order reaction is a reaction which is expected from its rate law to be of a higher order, but which is found experimentally to follow first order kinetics. This happens when one of the reactants is present in such large excess that its concentration does not change appreciably during the reaction.

For example, in the hydrolysis of methyl acetate,

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3(aq) + H_2O(\mathit{l}) \longrightarrow CH_3COOH(aq) + CH_3OH(aq)}\)

the rate law is rate \(= k'[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}][\mathrm{H_2O}]\), so the reaction is expected to be of second order. Water is the solvent and is present in large excess, so \([\mathrm{H_2O}]\) stays effectively constant and may be written as a constant \(k''\). The rate law then becomes

rate \(= k'\,k''\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}] = k\,[\mathrm{CH_3COOCH_3}]\)  where \(k = k'\,k''\)

which contains one concentration term only, so the reaction is of first order.

**Integrated rate law for a zero order reaction.** A zero order reaction is one whose rate does not depend on the concentration of the reactant. For

\(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow P}\)

the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)

Rearranging,

\(d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\,dt\)

Let \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) be the concentration of A at \(t = 0\) and \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) its concentration at time \(t\). Integrating between these limits,

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t} d[\mathrm{A}] = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\([\mathrm{A}]_t - [\mathrm{A}]_0 = -k\,t\)

\(\therefore k\,t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t\)  and  \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]_t}{t}\)

which is the integrated rate law for a zero order reaction. Written as \([\mathrm{A}]_t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - k\,t\) it shows that a plot of \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) against \(t\) is a straight line of slope \(-k\) and intercept \([\mathrm{A}]_0\). Since \(k\) is a concentration divided by a time, its units are \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\), the same as those of the rate itself.

answer:
For a first order reaction the integrated rate law, written for the time, is

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

Take the initial amount of the reactant as \(100\).

**Time for \(90\%\) completion.** If \(90\%\) has reacted, \(10\%\) remains, so \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 10\) and

\(t_{90} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{10} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10} 10 = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 1 = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\)

**Time for \(99.9\%\) completion.** If \(99.9\%\) has reacted, \(0.1\%\) remains, so \([\mathrm{A}]_t = 0.1\) and

\(t_{99.9} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10}\dfrac{100}{0.1} = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log_{10} 1000 = \dfrac{2.303}{k} \times 3 = \dfrac{3 \times 2.303}{k}\)

**Ratio of the two times.** Dividing one by the other, the factor \(\dfrac{2.303}{k}\) cancels:

\(\dfrac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}} = \dfrac{3 \times 2.303/k}{2.303/k} = 3\)

\(\therefore t_{99.9} = 3\,t_{90}\)

The time required for \(99.9\%\) completion is three times the time required for \(90\%\) completion. The rate constant has cancelled, so the result holds for every first order reaction whatever its value of \(k\).
twin: Show that time required for \(99.9\%\) completion of a first order reaction is three times the time required for \(90\%\) completion.

answer:
Let the rate law for \(\mathrm{A + B \longrightarrow P}\) be

rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\)   ...... (i)

where \(x\) and \(y\) are the orders of the reaction with respect to A and to B.

**First observation.** \([\mathrm{B}]\) is doubled at constant \([\mathrm{A}]\) and the rate doubles:

\(2 \times\) rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[2\mathrm{B}]^y = k\,2^y[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\)   ...... (ii)

Dividing (ii) by (i), the factor \(k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\) cancels:

\(2 = 2^y\), so \(y = 1\)

**Second observation.** \([\mathrm{A}]\) is trebled and \([\mathrm{B}]\) doubled, and the rate becomes six times as large:

\(6 \times\) rate \(= k[3\mathrm{A}]^x[2\mathrm{B}]^y = k\,3^x\,2^y[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\)   ...... (iii)

Dividing (iii) by (i),

\(6 = 3^x \times 2^y\)

Substituting \(y = 1\),

\(6 = 3^x \times 2\), so \(3^x = 3\) and \(x = 1\)

\(\therefore\) the rate law equation is rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\)

The reaction is first order in A, first order in B and of second order overall. The result reproduces both observations: doubling \([\mathrm{B}]\) alone doubles the product \([\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\), and trebling \([\mathrm{A}]\) while doubling \([\mathrm{B}]\) multiplies it by \(3 \times 2 = 6\), exactly as stated.
twin: Consider, \(\mathrm{A + B \longrightarrow P}\). If the concentration of A is doubled with \([\mathrm{B}]\) being constant, the rate of the reaction doubles. If the concentration of A is tripled and that of B is doubled, the rate increases by a factor \(6\). What is order of the reaction with respect to each reactant? Determine the overall order of the reaction.

answer:
**(A)** zero

For a reaction of overall order \(n\) the rate law is

rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^n\), so \(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\)

The rate of a reaction always has the units \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\) and a concentration the units \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), so the units of the rate constant are

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}}{(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}})^{n}} = \mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ dm^{3n-3}\ s^{-1}}\)

Matching this against the given units \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\) requires the index of mol to be \(1\), that is \(1 - n = 1\)

\(\therefore n = 0\)

Substituting the other orders into the same expression confirms it: first order gives \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), second order \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ dm^{3}\ s^{-1}}\) and third order \(\mathrm{mol^{-2}\ dm^{6}\ s^{-1}}\), none of which is \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\). Only for a zero order reaction are the units of the rate constant the same as those of the rate, because the rate is then equal to \(k\) itself.

answer:
For a first order reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow products}\) the differential rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]\)

Separating the variables and integrating between the initial concentration \([\mathrm{A}]_0\) at \(t = 0\) and the concentration \([\mathrm{A}]_t\) at time \(t\),

\(\displaystyle\int_{[\mathrm{A}]_0}^{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = -k\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t} dt\)

\(\ln\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_t}{[\mathrm{A}]_0} = -k\,t\)

which on converting to logarithms to base \(10\) gives the integrated rate law

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t}\)

**The half life.** The half life \(t_{1/2}\) of a reaction is the time in which the concentration of the reactant falls to one half of its initial value. Hence when \(t = t_{1/2}\),

\([\mathrm{A}]_t = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2}\)

Substituting this condition into the integrated rate law,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_0/2}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log_{10} 2 = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}} \times 0.3010\)

\(\therefore k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)  and  \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

which is the required relation. The initial concentration has cancelled from the result, so the half life of a first order reaction is independent of how much reactant was taken to begin with, and depends only on the rate constant.

answer:
**The Arrhenius equation.** Arrhenius found from experiment that the rate constant of a reaction varies with temperature as

\(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\)   ...... (i)

where \(k\) is the rate constant, \(E_a\) the activation energy, \(R\) the gas constant \(8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(T\) the temperature in kelvin and \(\mathrm{A}\) the pre-exponential or frequency factor, which for a first order reaction has the same unit as \(k\).

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides of (i),

\(\ln k = \ln \mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}\)

Dividing the logarithmic terms by \(2.303\) to convert them to base \(10\),

\(\log_{10} k = \log_{10}\mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T}\)   ...... (ii)

Equation (ii) is of the form \(y = mx + c\), with \(y = \log_{10}k\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{T}\). A plot of \(\log_{10}k\) against \(\dfrac{1}{T}\) is therefore a straight line whose slope is \(-\dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\) and whose intercept is \(\log_{10}\mathrm{A}\), from which

\(E_a = -2.303\,R \times \text{slope}\)

**Expression for the variation of the rate constant with temperature.** Let \(k_1\) be the rate constant at temperature \(T_1\) and \(k_2\) that at temperature \(T_2\). Writing equation (ii) at each temperature,

\(\log_{10} k_1 = \log_{10}\mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T_1}\)   ...... (iii)

\(\log_{10} k_2 = \log_{10}\mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T_2}\)   ...... (iv)

The activation energy and the pre-exponential factor do not change with temperature, so subtracting (iii) from (iv) removes \(\log_{10}\mathrm{A}\):

\(\log_{10} k_2 - \log_{10} k_1 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T_1} - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T_2}\)

\(\therefore \log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1\,T_2}\right)\)

This is the required expression. For \(T_2 > T_1\) the right hand side is positive, so \(k_2 > k_1\): the rate constant, and with it the rate of the reaction, increases as the temperature is raised, and for a given rise in temperature the increase is the greater the larger the activation energy.

answer:
The two quantities supplied are \(4 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), whose unit is that of the pre-exponential factor of a first order reaction, and \(98.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), whose unit is that of an activation energy. The solution is worked with

\(\mathrm{A} = 4 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)  and  \(E_a = 98.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} = 98.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)

this being the only reading on which the data are dimensionally consistent, since a half life cannot have the unit \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

**The rate constant required.** For a first order reaction

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\)

\(t_{1/2} = 10\ \mathrm{minutes} = 10 \times 60 = 600\ \mathrm{s}\)

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{600\ \mathrm{s}} = 1.155 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

**The temperature.** The Arrhenius equation \(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) is written as

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,T}\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{1.155 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 3.463 \times 10^{16}\)

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \log_{10}(3.463 \times 10^{16}) = 16.54\)

Rearranging for \(T\) and substituting \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\),

\(T = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R\,\log_{10}(\mathrm{A}/k)} = \dfrac{98.6 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 16.54}\)

\(= \dfrac{98.6 \times 10^{3}}{316.7}\)

\(\therefore T = 311.3\ \mathrm{K} = 38.3\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

Substituting this temperature back into the Arrhenius equation checks the answer:

\(\dfrac{E_a}{R\,T} = \dfrac{98.6 \times 10^{3}}{8.314 \times 311.3} = 38.10\)

\(k = 4 \times 10^{13} \times e^{-38.10} = 1.14 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.14 \times 10^{-3}} = 6.1 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{s}\), that is about \(10\) minutes, which is the half life asked for.

answer:
A zero order reaction is a reaction whose rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant, so that the rate remains unchanged for as long as any reactant is present.

For the reaction \(\mathrm{A \longrightarrow P}\) the rate law is

rate \(= -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)

The rate is therefore numerically equal to the rate constant, so the units of \(k\) are the units of the rate itself, \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\). Integration gives \([\mathrm{A}]_t = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - k\,t\), so a plot of the concentration of the reactant against time is a straight line of slope \(-k\).

The decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure is an example: the surface is completely covered with ammonia molecules, so adding more ammonia does not increase the rate.
